items.q: What kind of region does this survey map?
options: A perceptual region, defined by what people believe
A formal region: it is defined by one trait that is measured
A functional region: it is organized around a center
A transition zone: it is defined by a change in climate

why.correct: Perceptual (vernacular) regions are defined by people's feelings and beliefs, so surveys are a good way to map them.
options: Right: the region exists in people's minds, so it is measured by asking them.
A formal region rests on a measured trait, such as a language most people speak; this rests on opinions.
Nothing here is organized around a center or tied by trips to it.
The survey is about what people believe, not about climate.

items.q: Describe the edge of "the North" shown on this map.
options: Sharp: each province is either fully in the region or fully out of it, with no middle
Fuzzy: in the Central Valley and Western Uplands, residents are split
It follows the South Coast, where most people say that they belong to the North
It is a straight line that a government drew across the country

why.correct: Regions often have transition zones at their edges, where the trait or belief that defines them fades.
options: Several provinces fall in the middle classes, so the edge is not sharp.
Right: provinces in the middle classes form a transition zone, where the region fades out.
The South Coast is in the lowest class.
The survey measures beliefs; no government line appears.

items.q: Which province is most clearly at the heart of "the North"?
options: The Central Valley
The South Coast
The Northern Hills
The Capital Region

why.correct: The heart of a perceptual region is where the most people agree they belong.
options: The Central Valley is in a middle class: residents are split.
The South Coast is in the lowest class, under 20%.
Right: it is in the top class, 80% or more.
The Capital Region is in the second-lowest class.

items.q: What is a limitation of this survey as a map of "the North"?
options: It is quantitative, so it says nothing about what people believe
It uses a choropleth, which is the wrong kind of map for showing percents
It shows an invented country, so the region it maps is not a real one to study
One value per province hides towns whose views differ from their province

why.correct: Data by province are aggregated: name what they hide at a smaller scale.
options: The survey turns beliefs into percents; that is a fair way to measure them.
Choropleth maps suit percents well.
Invented places are fine for practice; the limit is the size of the units.
Right: provincial averages can hide a northern-minded valley inside a southern province.

items.q: The commuters tie these provinces to the capital. What kind of region do they define?
options: A functional region, organized around the capital
A formal region, where everyone shares one language
A perceptual region, drawn from what residents believe
A transition zone between two climates

why.correct: Functional (nodal) regions are defined by flows to and from a center: commuters, deliveries, phone calls, newspaper readers.
options: Right: a functional region is tied together by trips, trade or services focused on a center.
The map measures trips, not a shared trait such as a language.
The data are counts of trips, not beliefs.
Climate is not part of the map.

items.q: Describe the pattern of commuting on this map.
options: The most commuters come from the Western Uplands, one of the provinces farthest away
Most come from the Central Valley, next to the capital; fewest from the far north and west
About the same number of commuters come from each of the seven provinces shown
The fewest commuters come from the provinces next to the capital

why.correct: In a functional region, ties are strongest near the center and weaken with distance.
options: The Western Uplands have one of the smallest circles.
Right: the circles shrink with distance from the capital, a sign of distance decay.
The circles range from 5 to 60 thousand.
The neighboring provinces have the largest circles.

items.q: A fast train line opens from the Western Uplands to the capital. How would this region most likely change?
options: It would shrink, because faster trains push the capital away
It would turn into a formal region, because a train is one trait
It would reach farther west as more Western Uplands residents commute
It would stay the same, because regions keep the shape they were given

why.correct: Functional regions change shape when transport changes: time-space compression stretches them.
options: Faster trains bring places closer in time, not farther.
A train line connects places; it is not a shared trait of the people.
Right: faster travel cuts the time to the center, so more people can commute from farther away.
Functional regions grow and shrink as links to the center change.

items.q: In Quebec, Canada, a large majority of people speak French as their first language. Which kind of region is Quebec in this sense?
options: A functional region
A perceptual region
A transition zone
A formal region

why.correct: A formal (uniform) region shares one or more measurable traits, such as language, climate or a main crop.
options: A functional region is tied to a center by flows, not defined by a shared trait.
A perceptual region rests on beliefs; language can be measured.
A transition zone is the fuzzy edge of a region, not the region itself.
Right: a formal region shares a measurable trait, here the main language.

items.q: Which is the best example of a functional region?
options: The area a Denver newspaper delivers to each morning
The area where most people speak Spanish in the United States
The area Americans call "the Midwest"
The area where corn is the main crop in the United States

why.correct: Functional regions are organized around a center: a newspaper, an airport, a store, a city.
options: Right: it is defined by deliveries from one center, Denver.
A shared language makes a formal region.
A region defined by what people call it is perceptual.
A shared main crop makes a formal region.

items.q: Ask Americans which states are in "the South" and you get different answers. Why?
options: It is a formal region with a border set in federal law, which people forget
It is a perceptual region, so its edges depend on what each person believes
It is a functional region tied to one city, Atlanta, by daily commuting
It is not a region, since it has no clear edges that everyone can agree on

why.correct: Perceptual (vernacular) regions are shaped by culture, history and the media, and people draw them differently.
options: No law sets the region's edges.
Right: perceptual regions are real in people's minds, and minds differ, so the edges blur.
The South is not defined by trips to one city.
Regions with fuzzy edges are still regions; most regions have them.

items.q: Compare a formal region and a functional region.
options: Both are defined by what people believe about a place
A formal region is tied to a center, whereas a functional region shares a trait
Formal regions share a trait, whereas functional regions are tied to a center
Both have sharp edges that stay fixed as transport and trade change over time

why.correct: A compare answer speaks of both: formal by a shared trait, functional by ties to a center.
options: Beliefs define perceptual regions, not these two.
This swaps the two definitions.
Right: it says something about both and names the difference.
Both kinds usually have fuzzy edges, and functional regions change as links change.

items.q: The Sahel is a belt across Africa south of the Sahara, where desert slowly gives way to grassland. What kind of area is the Sahel?
options: A functional region organized around one city
A perceptual region drawn by surveys
A sharp line between the desert and the grassland
A transition zone between two formal regions

why.correct: Edges between regions are usually zones where one set of traits gives way to another.
options: The Sahel is defined by climate and plants, not trips to a center.
It is mapped from rainfall and plants, not from beliefs.
The change happens across a wide belt, not at a line.
Right: the dry climate fades into a wetter one across hundreds of kilometers.

items.q: Some definitions of "the Middle East" include Egypt and Türkiye; others leave out one or both. What does this show about regions?
options: People draw regions for a purpose, so their edges can differ and be contested
The Middle East has no countries, so it is not a real region
There is one official map of the region, and the others are mistakes
Regions are set by the United Nations, and its map settles the argument

why.correct: Regions are generalizations: different people draw them differently, so their edges can overlap and be contested.
options: Right: who draws a region, and why, shapes where its edges go.
The region clearly includes countries; the argument is about which ones.
No single official map of the Middle East exists.
Regions are tools people make, and their edges are often debated.

items.q: Which of these are regions at the local scale? Select all that apply.
options: The delivery area of a pizza shop in Toronto
A neighborhood in Lagos known for its markets
Southeast Asia
The European Union

why.correct: Regions exist at every scale, from a neighborhood to a group of countries.
options: Right: one shop's delivery area lies inside one city.
Right: a neighborhood lies inside one city.
Southeast Asia is a region at the regional scale: many countries.
The European Union joins many countries, so it is far larger than local.

items.q: Build a sentence that identifies a region, its type and the trait or tie that defines it.

specific.model: The area served by Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson airport is a functional region, because travelers from many nearby towns fly in and out through that one center.

region.label: Region
options: The area served by Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson airport
Some area

why.1: Too vague: name a real region.

type.label: Type
options: functional
formal
perceptual

why.1: A formal region shares a trait; the airport's area is tied by trips to a center.
why.2: A perceptual region rests on beliefs; this area is defined by travel to the airport.

tie.label: What defines it
options: travelers from many nearby towns fly in and out through that one center
it has a large airport

why.1: Having an airport is a feature; the region is defined by the trips people make to it.

why.correct: Name the region, its type and the trait or tie that defines it, with "because".
